title: Socialists Must Change Today’s World
author: Joan Roelofs
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/07/IMG_7860-680x508.jpeg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

Socialism is more favorably viewed these days, especially by younger people.
What is socialism? Nobody knows. There is no official definition of socialism.
Diverse ideas, institutions, and several nations have been considered
socialist. Whatever variety, socialism needs to confront the world of today.
It must relate to our most urgent problems, not merely those of the 1820s
(many still with us) when the term first appeared from critics of society.
Even so, we can learn from history: ideas, experiments, and efforts to create
socialist nations.

Here are some thoughts, not a complete manifesto, from the perspective of an
eclectic ecosocialist. Of the problems, war is the worst, as it threatens
human existence; kills, wounds, and poisons millions of people; and devastates
the environment even by its preparations. Resources the world over are
increasingly devoted to military arsenals, institutions, and propaganda rather
than human and planetary survival; militarism is growing in culture, economy,
society, and education. War enables fantastic profits for some industries, and
serves capitalism generally by distracting people from exploitative and unjust
economic systems, yet it is a threat to all. How do socialists propose to end
war?

Industrialization and urbanization also degrade an environment that needs to
sustain human health and well-being. There is enough labor, now wasted on war
and other destructive as well as frivolous industries, to say nothing of
idleness. For a socialist society, the occupational structure must be
drastically reformed, and the many affected must be retrained, relocated, or
retired, and provided with a copious standard of living. Many workers in any
case would be surplus in a socialist economy—not simply due to AI. In addition
to those employed in war industries, there are millions in finance, real
estate, insurance, and advertising (including robo callers). The vast array of
the NGO world, much of which exists to humanize, prop up, or denounce
capitalism, would also be greatly diminished.

Now many worldwide make a living from criminal activities: prostitution,
pornography, illegal drugs, gambling, scams, smuggling, and other rackets.
This has also increased the workforce of police, detectives, prisons, and
crime reporters. We can’t simply enable proletarians to own or control the
existing means of production; we have to produce for the good life.

A supersize crew is producing and dispensing junk food and junk of all kinds.
Fashion, boutiques, and fads waste resources, energy, and labor, and produce
voluminous waste themselves. Elaborate wedding decorations often last longer
than the marriages, and commercial holiday paraphernalia supports booming
industries, including fireworks. Hobbies that do not enhance the common good,
health, safety, or the environment are nevertheless a source of income for
some workers, e.g., children’s flight instructors.

Today’s workers include entertainers of all types: professional athletes,
ballerinas, stand-up comics, et al. Those in the arts may love their work, but
many are struggling to make a living. Tourism is a major polluting industry,
and its workers are often deprived of rights, decent wages, and benefits. How
do we socialize these kinds of work?

Now there are numerous retired people, and those disabled, dropped out, or
homeless. Socialists must figure out a way to integrate them into society. The
most exploited workers, including undocumented immigrants and many foreign
contract workers, should not be expelled, but their situations must be
changed.

Obvious problems and well-reported are the deplorable amount of poverty and
homelessness in a supposedly rich country. Also, affecting even the well-off,
our infrastructure is crumbling. Schools, even private ones, are infused with
decaying and toxic materials, medical care is shrinking and often many miles
away, and violent crime is normal.

I am not suggesting that fun, arts, frivolity, leisure, or sports be
abolished—only that they be redistributed. Necessary work to feed, clothe,
house, educate and maintain the health of the world’s population and the
restoration of the earth should be shared by everyone. It is not enough to
provide equality of income; status and labor must be greatly equalized. This
was a principle of the brilliant, somewhat mad, pre-Marxian socialist,
[Charles
Fourier](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/fourier/index.htm).

We need to protect and reclaim land (and possibly the seas) to provide clean
food and water for the world, as well as clothing, building materials,
medicines, and some of our energy needs. Even if organically grown, food
transported long distances is chemicalized, and all use much fuel and
infrastructure. Before we revert to lab-produced food we can better use the
resources we have; the [_Centrality of
Agriculture_](https://books.google.com/books?id=c0ZcTTXw9a8C&pg=PA10&source=gbs_toc_r&cad=1#v=onepage&q&f=false)
deserves more consideration by socialists.

The family needs reconstruction, as it is not doing well in its supposed
traditional functions, while those who have little or none of it are also in
need. The increase in one-person households puts great stress on housing and
resources, and not contributing much joy. Housing is so obviously unsuited to
the “free market.” It is not simply a problem of “greedy landlords” as many
moderate-income people buy up houses for the rental income. “Demand” can
rarely produce an affordable “supply.”

Perhaps not unprecedented but now more obvious is the chronic unhappiness
affecting people of all income levels. The use of antidepressants, other legal
drugs, and illegal ones is considerable, and surprising in the countries that
are most affluent and are considered most democratic. Children, remarkably in
the great U.S., continue to be beset with homicide, suicide, chronic illness,
bullying, exploitation, sexual and physical abuse, depression, and loneliness.

Equality in wealth is especially important for political power; democracy does
not work in nations or institutions where there is a vast difference in
resources. Not only is every kind of propaganda, education and civil society
organization financed by the wealthy, even progressive and radical political
candidates can be co-opted. There are many other ills of the world; these are
mentioned here because they don’t get much attention in current socialist
discussion.

What can we learn from history? Early socialists were somewhat “reactionary,”
seeking to restore values that had been lost. Some regarded the monastic
structure as a model of a cooperative economy, not only for those choosing a
life of poverty and celibacy. Along with community and security for single and
aged people, they were generators of technological innovation and high-grade
crafts. Socialists wanted to universalize the positive aspects of such
communities for a population that reproduces, for they did not believe that
the end was near. Marx and Engels were impressed by the Shakers’ economic
structure, although not their reproductive rules. The pre-Marxist French
socialists were in part motivated by a desire to replace the ideals of
Catholicism (however unrealized), as after the Revolution a new national
ideology seemed necessary.

Unpopular and neglected ideas and practices, often dismissed as not socialism
at all, may furnish useful clues for our times. Charles Fourier cataloged the
ills of society that needed to be remedied—not only economic ones. He thought
war was the most horrible and wasteful aspect of humanity.

He regarded the laissez-faire economy as a prime cause of misery that the
French Revolution had not merely overlooked, but had intensified. Furthermore,
and very relevant to today’s all-class drugged “brave new world” he thought
the “free” market hurt all people. He also believed that there could not even
be liberal democracy in a nation if there were a class of people condemned to
menial work for their entire lives. Unrelenting physical toil as well as
generally boring work suppressed the true human multidimensional personality.
Everyone should perform some of the necessary tasks; the type could be chosen
according to one’s proclivities. Furthermore, a Fourierist diet, based on
market gardening and small animals, would require less land than field crops
and large animal pastures. It would also be “attractive labor.”

Fourier’s observations of domestic life led him to conclude that marriage and
the family were the source of much unhappiness and dysfunction, as well as
environmental stress due to wasted resources for heating and furnishing
individual households. In his ideal communities (called phalansteries) all
non-violent sexual orientations (for adults only) were not only accepted but
often facilitated

Fourier’s ideas (cleaned up) infused the U.S. 19th century communitarian
societies via his disciple, Victor Considerant, whose work was translated and
propagated by journalist Albert Brisbane. Brisbane had a thrice-weekly column
in _The New York Tribune_ and an influential 1840 book, [_The Social Destiny
of Man_](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/fourier/social-
destiny.pdf). The
“[Associationist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Union_of_Associationists)”
movement of Fourierists was a broad church, which included fundamentalist
Christians and atheistic socialists. The communities, especially the longer-
lived religious societies, offered more personal security, social services,
health and dental care than that experienced by the general population. Ageing
members could be cared for by the whole community rather than the sole
responsibility of a family member; many elders didn’t even have such a person.

A number of the communities deliberately created a “new improved model” of the
family. This was the case of the Shakers, the Mormons, and the Oneida
Community. There are memoirs and archives that can give us a rounded view of
how these worked out, and what useful tips we might gain for family reform or
replacement.

Appropriate technology was not shunned (unlike the Amish who were not
communal). Although some of the communities relocated because of adverse
conditions, members regarded their land and structures as permanent assets to
be protected, in contrast to the common method of individual Western
settlement: use up the land, sell the place, and move on. All eyes could
observe work hazards or domestic violence so there was more protection than in
the isolated family farm. These were not communities nostalgic for peasant
life, although some of the religious societies believed that the “saved”
should withdraw from a wicked world. Many communities saw themselves as models
to be followed for settling the country while avoiding the evils of slavery or
capitalism. They were the 19th century counterparts of agro-industrial
communities; strongly influenced by negative experiences and reports of
conditions in 19th century cities.

Sharing of necessary work was generally a principle and sometimes succeeded.
Notable was the pacifism of most communities, opposing militarism as well as
nationalism. There is no denying that they were often situated on land
illegally seized from Native Americans. In addition, only the Shakers and the
short-lived Nashoba community had black members. We can still learn from their
positive practices. These experiments might be more studied by socialists had
Zinn mentioned them in his [_People’s
History_](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0062397346?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback).

Another source of ideas for today, the British Fabians, made detailed plans
for converting existing institutions to socialism. These included transforming
industries into control by local or national government, and a parliament for
the environment. Fabian G. B. Shaw wrote that he wouldn’t mind performing his
national service by washing dishes for a few hours a day; he could be
scrubbing pots and thinking of plots. Others have suggested that a “service
tax” could be paid by working for a few weeks each year, or for one year full-
time, etc., as one’s preferences dictated.

The Fabians also advocated for personal freedom, and supported gradual,
peaceful, change rather than violent revolution. Even Lenin found some Fabian
ideas useful for creating a socialist economy. Granted there were some Fabians
who were racist, imperialist, perhaps antisemitic, but these negative views do
not negate the useful ideas. They have also been held by Marxists and other
socialists.

What we can learn from the history of Marxism: how was it able persuade so
many people of different lands and statuses (not merely the proletariat) to
act for radical change, often at great risk to their lives and current status?
How can we motivate the many who are doing ok or others so demoralized and
propagandized that they don’t see any hope for radical change?

In past and current socialist countries there were major failures, some
horrific. Exploitation and immiseration often resulted from very rapid
[industrialization](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0520208234?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback),
which was prompted by ideology as well as a realistic expectation of military
attack. As in the capitalist democracies, there was repression of those
suspected of subverting the system. However, disaffection was magnified by
overt and covert interventions by the capitalist nations and organizations,
and effective consumerist propaganda.

The project of transforming traditional cultural traits into those of a “new
socialist person” was not very successful, and younger generations were barely
aware of pre-revolutionary miseries. Nevertheless, these nations were (and
are) trying to implement socialism. They provided a better life for the many
than their situation before and after, especially for women, minorities, poor
peasants, workers, and pensioners.

The socialist nations employed varied forms of ownership—national, local,
cooperative, public and privately owned housing, small businesses, allotment
gardens, et al. Collective farms worked well in some countries. Cuba
discovered that some crops were better suited to national ownership, e.g.,
livestock breeding and sugar, and others were better as collectives or
private, e.g., tobacco. Mongolia herded herders into collectives, but they
worked there for only a limited number of days and also owned animals for
their own profit.

Although a deviation from the strict equality demanded by some socialist
theories, the provision of a basic income for all was often supplemented with
incentives for amount and quality of work. There was a safety net for co-
operative workers or collective farm workers, whose income could vary because
of weather, pests, or market changes. The basics for all workers might include
housing, health care, education, parental leave, and pensions; and also
subsidized transportation, entertainment, and vacations. There were fancy
resorts and apartment complexes with pools, theaters, et al for the elite
(political, artistic, or athletic). However, by the 1980s most people e. g.,
in the USSR, could engage in sports (equipment provided), go to sanitoria, or
vacate at a dacha with garden space, which were often former country houses
divided into small apartments.

The young pioneer organizations aimed to integrate and socialize children of
all backgrounds. They provided constructive activities for children’s free
time, along with sports, art, music, dance, and fun, but also military
training. Urie Bronfenbrenner’s 1970 [_Two Worlds of
Childhood_](https://www.amazon.com/Two-Worlds-Childhood-U-S-U-S-
S-R/dp/0871541688/ref=sr_1_1?crid=2FS1LX8DAJI92&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.oolVYR2_6aCsTu1eZbq0GvgYx2kPuub7zcjPyImVJk6J6B-_0IktMv9LMaWol4KIRYW4ItTkE04be46WyKrwFx08yXVot5kAYQknu9Ytdnhk2vjD9-31pVwRJpvqM3XoAalK-
SCh3IxEw7BoxbszuDlnvThjNUFVisw5eAR8DHBsplBbGmdG_DORTwHopleCNIl-
WAMjWbAuQMaGS2sBURFBuY-
aAsMnWb2WcSeqQVY.qThYC75PuPeYO7pl_d5yUgi4_-mm5zjLSMIoRnyebpY&dib_tag=se&keywords=Two+worlds+of+childhood&qid=1784235220&s=books&sprefix=two+worlds+of+childhood%2Cstripbooks%2C139&sr=1-1)
contrasts USSR and US children’s socialization:

Dr. Bronfenbrenner finds that the Soviet child, both in and out of school,
grows up in an environment that encourages him to look beyond his own
immediate gratification to the needs and expectations of Soviet society. By
contrast, the American child is exposed to a largely accidental process of
development by which he is actually brought up by his peers, in an atmosphere
pervaded by subtle opposition to the standards of adult society, and by the
ubiquitous television set which significantly contributes to his potential for
antisocial behavior. (John H. Fischer, Teachers College, Columbia University.
Blub on book back.)

In 1983, Soviet educator Yuri Azarov, in _A Book About Bringing Up Children,_
argued that if children were left alone in their spare time there would be
bullying, gangs, ostracism, and other anti-social behavior; gang or clique
members would be subject to the despotism of the “leaders.” He maintained that
children’s leisure time should be directed by adults. In view of U.S.
children’s shocking situation today, subjection to adult authority is surely a
lesser evil.

Socialist nations’ experiments in abolishing the division of labor were not
very impressive, but we can learn from them. In Kazakhstan, office workers
were released to join the cotton harvest; in China academic students took a
turn working in the countryside; some liked it so much that they gave up their
elite education and stayed there. These and other arrangements involved
coercion, but the invisible hand of capitalism’s supply and demand has never
produced free choice of occupation for the many. Slaves, expropriated and
indigenous people, indentured servants, immigrants, landless peasants, and
others with no options have done the demeaning and dangerous work. It is still
a goal of socialism to permit full expression of the human personality, not
only in leisure time but also in work.

There is open land in the US and many other countries although it is often
degraded. While millions are overworked, human labor is an underutilized
source of energy; many people do no physical work or else expend their energy
in sports and gyms. Agriculture, now highly industrialized at the expense of
human health, fossil fuel and fertile soil, needs more workers—and much
shorter work hours. This suggests a Fourierist solution to problems resulting
from globalization, industrial agriculture, meaningless work, loneliness, and
the decline of community.

Despite Fourier’s arguments for voluntarism, it is unlikely that necessary
work can be accomplished without planning and coercion. How planning could be
carried out and democratically structured remains a mystery, although
information technology might obviate some of the past planning dysfunctions.

Coercion can be fairly gentle, especially when compared to military service
where even if one doesn’t get near an enemy, maimed or killed, one faces harsh
training, pollution, and hazing. It can be a more democratic tax than the
current situation, whereby many have no freedom and others lots of it. With
appropriate technology, short shifts, and attention to health and safety, work
could be less onerous. Furthermore, choice can be offered. We have clues based
on what people do voluntarily: garden, make things, hike, fix things, care for
people, make them laugh, et al. The resulting spare time could be devoted to
art, music, drama, standup comic, needlework, loafing, healthful sports, etc.,
or philosophizing about the next improvements of society.

As for war, who knows. It existed before capitalism. Socialist nations
generally refrain from starting foreign wars, although they have used violence
in defense and civil wars. Fourier proposed Peace Corps-like alternatives to
war. Competition, adventure, and consensual sexual activities would engage
world armies and crusades would be dedicated to environmental restoration. His
scenario has been translated as [_The World War of Small
Pastries_](https://archive.org/details/TheWorldWarOfSmallPasteriesByCharlesFourier).
In a similar spirit, almost a century later, William James proposed a “[Moral
Equivalent of
War](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Popular_Science_Monthly/Volume_77/October_1910/The_Moral_Equivalent_of_War).”

If now—and this is my idea—there were, instead of mil­itary conscription, a
conscription of the whole youthful population to form for a certain number of
years a part of the army enlisted against Nature, the injustice [of
inequal­ity in toil] would tend to be evened out, and numerous other goods to
the commonwealth would follow.

James’ “youth army” would surely require some modification in the light of
today’s values. We wouldn’t want a corps that was enlisted “against Nature,”
but one that worked with nature and appropriate technology to achieve the best
outcomes for humans and the planet. James also ignored the psychological needs
of women, whose role has often been that of supporting the male warriors. A
civilian corps would need to be inclusive, all races, all genders, new
immigrants and Mayflower descendants, three-homers and homeless. James was
concerned that “development” activities would not be considered he­roic
enough. Today both ecological dev­astation and rampant, planet-threatening
militarism require superhuman efforts.

Here’s one suggestion. Primary education for all would include a half day of
the usual subjects, including indoor learning such as computer skills. In the
other half day children of all backgrounds would be assembled into groups
where they would learn the basics of growing, processing, and cooking food;
foraging for food, building materials, and medicinal herbs; sewing and care of
clothing; carpentry and maintenance skills; and nursing, child care, and elder
care. Directed by teachers, scientists (surplus from war work), craftspeople,
and indigenous people, the children might even invent some techniques. There
could be fun and games, even team sports if the teams are resorted each game.
At age 18 all would be drafted and serve three years according to preferences,
in child care, elder care, health aides, farming, forestry, remediation, food
service, and the small military necessary. They would work under the
supervision of experts, some from a national department of civilian
infrastructure rather than Army engineers. Pay would be adequate and shifts
short. Afterwards, they could attend college, professional or technical
training, or enter one of the occupations experienced. All would have reserve
army status, with a few weeks service required, or emergency work.

As James wrote: “The war against war is going to be no holiday excursion or
camping party.” Furthermore, remediating environmental damage and transforming
our food, fiber, and forestry systems will be no easy walk.
